The pressure is current, the status stakes are current, the hope or fear is current, and all of that can make the frame feel complete when it is actually narrow. A present-bound mind can confuse nearness with importance and intensity with clarity.

The chapter title suggests a way to widen that frame: adventures in mental time travel. On the thin authorized surface, the safest reading is that Duke is asking the reader to inspect a present decision from a later vantage point. Instead of letting today's room or mood act like the only judge, the thinker asks what a later self, a later review, or later evidence would notice that is easy to miss now. This is less about imagining the future as a fantasy landscape and more about challenging the dictatorship of immediacy.

That challenge matters because the present moment carries biases that do not always announce themselves. Social pressure can make a person call agreement wisdom. Short-term pain can make a setback look permanent. Current excitement can make a fragile forecast feel stronger than it is. A future-facing frame can weaken those distortions by asking how much of today's certainty would still look justified once the moment loses some of its emotional force.

This interpretation also fits the book's earlier logic. Pricing beliefs made confidence visible. Feedback from outcomes stopped one-shot verdict thinking. Buddies and dissent made private and group stories answer to outside pressure. The chapter likely needs a sharp limit because future perspective can be misused. A reader could turn it into fantasy, pretending that imagining a future self somehow grants real foresight. That would clash with the rest of the book, which repeatedly warns against false certainty. The more coherent reading is narrower: a future vantage point improves perspective but does not eliminate contingency. It makes current distortion easier to spot while keeping uncertainty intact.

That limit is what preserves the method's integrity. Mental time travel is useful if it helps the reader ask better questions now. What would later evidence make obvious? What current confidence claim might look too strong in retrospect? What part of today's room, clock, or mood is narrowing the frame? Those questions make the exercise disciplined instead of dreamy.
